In plain language: *When a transaction finishes a read or a write and the status returned is **OK**, the value it reads is either the value it has previously written in the same transaction, or the most recent value that was committed by some earlier transaction whose commit timestamp is less than or equal to the transaction’s read‑timestamp. A transaction cannot see a value written by a transaction that committed later than its own snapshot. Moreover, the log never contains two committed entries with the same key whose timestamps are not strictly ordered – any attempt to write a key that would break this ordering is detected as a write conflict and forces the transaction to roll back.* --- **SAFETY PROPERTY:** A transaction that ends with status **OK** always reads a value that either (1) was written by itself, or (2) was the latest committed value whose commit timestamp does not exceed the transaction’s read‑timestamp; consequently, no transaction can observe a write that was committed after its snapshot, and the log never contains conflicting writes to the same key at overlapping timestamps.

**System Overview**  
The model describes a small replicated‑state‑machine cluster that implements the Raft consensus algorithm together with a lease‑based read mechanism. The cluster consists of three server processes (named *n1*, *n2* and *n3*). Each server stores a log of client commands, participates in leader election, replicates log entries, and may grant time‑bounded read leases to clients. The model is deliberately bounded (maximum term, log length and clock value) so that the TLC model checker can explore all reachable states.

---

### Main Variables  

| Variable (conceptual) | Meaning in the system |
|-----------------------|-----------------------|
| **currentTerm[s]** (per server *s*) | The logical term number that server *s* believes the cluster is currently in. It is increased only when the server starts a new election. |
| **role[s]** (per server *s*) | The current Raft role of *s*: either *Follower* or *Leader*. A server becomes a candidate only internally during an election; the model records the final role after the election finishes. |
| **log[s]** (per server *s*) | An ordered list of log entries kept by *s*. Each entry contains three fields: a monotonically increasing *index*, the *term* in which the entry was created, and the client command (a *key*‑*value* pair). The length of every log is limited to **MaxLogLen** (four entries) for the model. |
| **commitIndex[s]** (per server *s*) | The highest log index that server *s* knows to be *committed* – i.e., replicated on a majority of servers and therefore safe to apply to the state machine. |
| **nextIndex[s][t]** (per leader *s* toward follower *t*) | For a leader, the index of the next log entry it will send to follower *t* when it issues an *AppendEntries* RPC. |
| **clock[s]** (per server *s*) | A logical timer that advances uniformly when the system “ticks”. It is used to compute lease expiration times. The clock value never exceeds **MaxClock** (seven) in the model. |
| **leaseExpiration[s]** (per leader *s*) | The logical time until which the current leader’s read lease is considered valid. It is set to *clock[s] + Delta* when the leader issues a lease. |
| **keySet** = {k1, k2} | The finite set of keys that clients may read or write. Each command in a log entry specifies one of these keys together with a new value. |
| **Delta** = 3 | The lease duration: a leader’s lease is valid for three clock ticks after it is granted. |
| **Epsilon** = 1 | The minimum gap required between a leader’s lease expiration and the next election timeout (used internally to avoid overlapping leases). |
| **Nil** | A distinguished constant representing “no value / no leader”. |

All of the above variables are implicitly part of the system state; the model checker treats them as mutable components that actions may read or update.

---

### Actions (State Transitions)  

1. **Init** – The initial state sets every server to term 0, role *Follower*, an empty log, commit index 0, and clock 0. No leader exists (leaseExpiration = Nil).  

2. **Election Timeout** – When a follower’s clock reaches a timeout threshold, the server increments its *currentTerm*, switches to *candidate* (internally) and sends *RequestVote* messages to all other servers. If a majority of servers grant their vote, the candidate becomes the unique *Leader* for that term and records a fresh lease (leaseExpiration = clock + Delta).  

3. **RequestVote / Vote** – A server receiving a *RequestVote* checks that the candidate’s term is at least as large as its own and that the candidate’s log is at least as up‑to‑date as its own. If both conditions hold, the server records its vote for the candidate.  

4. **AppendEntries (Log Replication)** – The leader periodically sends *AppendEntries* RPCs to each follower, containing the entries that the follower is missing (starting at *nextIndex*). A follower appends the received entries to its log if the preceding entry’s term and index match. The follower also updates its *commitIndex* to the leader’s *leaderCommit* field when it learns that a majority have stored an entry.  

5. **Client Write** – A client may issue a command (key k, value v) to the current leader. The leader creates a new log entry with the next index, the current term, and the (k, v) pair, appends it to its own log, and then starts replicating it via *AppendEntries*. The entry becomes *committed* as soon as a majority of servers acknowledge it.  

6. **Lease Grant** – After becoming leader, the server may periodically broadcast a *LeaseGrant* message that records a lease expiration time equal to *clock + Delta*. Followers store this expiration time; they consider the lease valid as long as their own clock is strictly less than the stored expiration.  

7. **Read Request** – A client may ask any server for the value of a key. If the server is a follower and its stored leaseExpiration is still in the future, it can serve the read directly from its local state machine (the value at the highest committed index for that key). If the lease is stale, the request must be forwarded to the current leader, which first ensures its lease is still valid before responding.  

8. **Clock Tick** – At each global step the model may increase the *clock* of any server by one, up to **MaxClock**. This models the passage of time and drives lease expiration and election timeouts.  

All of the above actions are combined into the **Next** relation that TLC explores.

---

### Invariants (Properties Checked by TLC)  

* **TypeOK** – All variables retain values of the expected type (e.g., *currentTerm* stays a natural number, *log* stays a list of entries, etc.).  
* **EntryIndexes** – Log indices are contiguous and start at 1; there are no gaps in any server’s log.  
* **OneLeaderPerTerm** – In any given term, at most one server has the role *Leader*.  
* **LeaderCompleteness** – If an entry is committed in term *t*, then every leader elected in a later term contains that entry in its log.  
* **StateMachineSafety** – Whenever two servers have committed entries at the same index, those entries are identical (same term, same key, same value). This guarantees that the replicated state machine never diverges.  
* **LinearizableReads** – A read that is served while the lease is valid returns the value of the most recent committed entry for the requested key, as if the read occurred atomically at some point between the client’s request and the lease expiration.  
* **BaitInv** – An auxiliary invariant used only for testing (it simply asserts that the model‑checking “level” stays below 99).  

---

### Symmetry  

The model declares **ServerSymmetry**, meaning that the three servers are interchangeable; TLC will treat any permutation of server identifiers as equivalent, reducing the number of distinct states it must explore.

---

### Safety Property  

**SAFETY PROPERTY:**  
The system guarantees that no two committed log entries at the same index can differ; consequently, once a command (a key‑value pair) is committed, that value is immutable and will be reflected by every future read, and there can never be more than one leader in the same term. This ensures that the replicated state machine remains consistent across all servers and that linearizable reads always return the latest committed value for a key.

**System Overview**

The model describes a very small distributed transaction system that follows the classic two‑phase commit (2PC) protocol. There are two kinds of processes:

* **Three Resource Managers (RMs)** – identified by the numbers 1, 2, 3.  
* **One Transaction Manager (TM)** – identified as process 0.

All communication is performed through a single shared data structure called **network**, which acts like a white‑board where any process can post a message and any other process can read the messages that are present. The network never loses messages; once a message is added it stays there for the rest of the execution.

---

### State Variables

| Variable | Meaning |
|----------|---------|
| **network** | The set of messages that have been posted. Each message records its type (`prepared`, `aborted`, `t‑commit`, `t‑abort`) and the identifier of the sender or intended receiver. |
| **rmState** | A map from each RM identifier to its current local state. The possible states are `working`, `prepared`, `committed`, and `aborted`. |
| **tmState** | The TM’s current phase: `unknown` (the initial state or after a failure), `commit` (has decided to commit), or `abort` (has decided to abort). |
| **informset** | The set of RMs that the TM still has to inform of its final decision. It is initialized to the full set `{1,2,3}` and shrinks as the TM delivers messages. |
| **pc** (program counter) | Internal bookkeeping used by the model to indicate which step each process is about to execute. It is not part of the functional description of the protocol. |

---

### Message Types

1. **`prepared`** – posted by an RM when it has finished its local work and is ready to commit. The message records the sender (`s`).  
2. **`aborted`** – posted by an RM that has aborted its local work. The message records the sender (`s`).  
3. **`t‑commit`** – posted by the TM to tell a particular RM that the global decision is **commit**. The message records the destination (`d`).  
4. **`t‑abort`** – posted by the TM to tell a particular RM that the global decision is **abort**. The message records the destination (`d`).  

All messages are immutable once placed in the network.

---

### Behaviour of a Resource Manager (RM)

An RM repeatedly executes the following loop while it is in either the `working` or `prepared` state:

1. **Prepare**  
   *Precondition*: the RM’s local state is `working`.  
   *Effect*: the RM changes its state to `prepared` and posts a `prepared` message on the network.

2. **Decide** (two alternatives)  

   *Commit branch*  
   - The RM waits until it observes a `t‑commit` message addressed to it.  
   - When such a message appears, the RM changes its state to `committed`. No further messages are posted.

   *Abort branch*  
   - The RM may either abort on its own (still in `working`) or react to a `t‑abort` message addressed to it.  
   - In either case the RM changes its state to `aborted` and posts an `aborted` message on the network.

The RM never moves out of the `committed` or `aborted` states.

---

### Behaviour of the Transaction Manager (TM)

The TM runs a single, linear sequence of steps:

1. **Wait for a global condition**  
   - **Commit possibility**: if **every** RM has already posted a `prepared` message (`canCommit`), the TM may proceed to the commit path.  
   - **Abort possibility**: if **any** RM has posted an `aborted` message (`canAbort`), the TM may proceed to the abort path.

2. **Commit path** (`TC`)  
   - The TM sets `tmState` to `commit`.  
   - It then repeatedly chooses a still‑uninformed RM from `informset`, posts a `t‑commit` message for that RM, and removes the RM from `informset`.  
   - This continues until `informset` becomes empty.  
   - (The model contains a flag `TMMAYFAIL` that could cause the TM to crash after sending a message; in the supplied configuration this flag is `FALSE`, so the TM never fails.)

3. **Abort path** (`TA`)  
   - The TM sets `tmState` to `abort`.  
   - It similarly iterates over `informset`, posting a `t‑abort` message for each remaining RM and removing that RM from the set, until the set is empty.

4. **Termination** (`TF`)  
   - After all RMs have been informed, the TM changes its state to `unknown` (a terminal state meaning “no longer participates”) and its program counter moves to `Done`.

The TM never sends both a commit and an abort message; the choice is made once, based on the global condition observed at the beginning of the transaction.

---

### Protocol Logic Summary

* The **first phase** (pre‑commit) consists of each RM optionally moving from `working` to `prepared` and announcing that it is ready.  
* The **second phase** (decision) is taken by the TM:  
  * If every RM is prepared, the TM decides **commit** and informs all RMs.  
  * If at least one RM has aborted, the TM decides **abort** and informs all RMs.  
* Each RM, upon receiving the TM’s decision, finalises its own state accordingly (`committed` or `aborted`).  
* All messages are stored in the shared `network`; there is no loss, duplication, or reordering beyond the nondeterministic order in which they are added.

---

### Safety Property (Invariant)

The model includes an invariant called **Consistent**. In plain English it guarantees that the system never reaches a state where two resource managers have made contradictory final decisions.

**SAFETY PROPERTY:**  
It is impossible for any resource manager to be in the `committed` state while another resource manager is in the `aborted` state; the protocol ensures that all resource managers either all commit or all abort, never a mixture of the two.

**System Overview**

The model describes a distributed transaction‑ordering service built on the *BPaxos* protocol, a variant of Paxos that uses a separate *dependency service* to allow commands that do not interfere with each other to be committed quickly. The system is composed of four kinds of processes:

| Process type | Instances | Role in the protocol |
|--------------|-----------|----------------------|
| **Dependency‑service replicas** | Five (named d1 … d5) | Store a table of which client commands depend on which earlier commands. When a command is submitted they compute and return the set of earlier commands that must be ordered before it. |
| **Acceptor replicas** | Five (named p1 … p5) | Participate in the two‑phase consensus primitive that underlies BPaxos. They store the highest round number they have seen and the value (command together with its dependency set) they have accepted for each instance. |
| **BPaxos replica (coordinator)** | One (named n1) | Acts as the proposer for a particular instance of the consensus algorithm. It talks to the dependency service to obtain a dependency set, then drives the acceptors through either the fast path or the classic path to reach a decision. |
| **Clients / commands** | Two distinct commands (named a and b) | Represent client operations that need to be ordered. The model declares that a and b *conflict* with each other, meaning they cannot both be decided for the same instance without respecting a defined ordering. |

All identifiers are treated as abstract values; the model does not attach any concrete payload to the commands other than their identity.

**Quorums**

The protocol relies on majority‑style quorums:

* A **dependency‑service quorum** consists of any three or more of the five dependency‑service replicas. A quorum response is sufficient to consider a dependency set authoritative.
* An **acceptor fast quorum** consists of any four or more acceptors. If a value is accepted by a fast quorum, the protocol can commit it without a second phase.
* An **acceptor classic quorum** consists of any three or more acceptors. This quorum is used in the ordinary two‑phase Paxos path (prepare → accept).

**Protocol Actions (high‑level description)**  

The model’s underlying module (not shown) defines the following actions that change the system state. Each action is atomic from the point of view of the model checker.

1. **ClientSubmit(cmd)** – A client issues a command *cmd* (either *a* or *b*). The command is placed in the proposer’s request queue together with a fresh instance identifier.

2. **RequestDependencies(inst, cmd)** – The coordinator *n1* sends the command *cmd* to all dependency‑service replicas. Each replica replies with the set of earlier commands it believes must precede *cmd*. When replies from a dependency‑service quorum are collected, the coordinator computes the *dependency set* for this instance (the union of the replies).

3. **FastPropose(inst, cmd, deps)** – Using the dependency set, the coordinator sends a *fast‑accept* message containing the triple *(instance, command, dependencies)* to all acceptors.  
   *If* an acceptor has not already promised a higher round number, it records the triple as its *fast‑accepted* value and replies with an acknowledgment.  
   When acknowledgments from a fast quorum arrive, the instance is **fast‑chosen** and the command can be committed immediately.

4. **ClassicPrepare(inst, round)** – If the fast path fails (e.g., not enough fast acknowledgments or a conflict is detected), the coordinator initiates the classic Paxos prepare phase. It sends the proposed round number to a classic quorum of acceptors. Each acceptor replies with the highest round and value it has already accepted for that instance.

5. **ClassicAccept(inst, round, cmd, deps)** – After receiving a majority of prepare replies, the coordinator selects the value with the highest round among the replies (or its own value if none were reported) and sends an *accept* request containing this value to a classic quorum. Acceptors that have not promised a higher round record the value as their *accepted* value and acknowledge.

6. **Commit(inst, cmd, deps)** – Once a value has been accepted by a classic quorum, the coordinator marks the instance as *chosen* and informs all replicas (including the dependency service) that the command is committed together with its dependency set. The command can then be executed after all commands in its dependency set have been executed.

7. **GarbageCollect(inst)** – After an instance is chosen and its command executed, the state associated with that instance may be removed from acceptors and the dependency service.

All actions respect the symmetry assumptions: the identifiers of replicas and commands can be permuted without affecting correctness, which allows the model checker to treat many states as equivalent.

**Key Variables (conceptual, not literal TLA+ names)**  

* *Instance table* – maps each instance identifier to a record containing the chosen command (if any), the dependency set, and the round number at which it was chosen.  
* *AcceptorState[p]* – for each acceptor *p*, stores the highest round seen and the value (command + dependencies) it has accepted in that round.  
* *DepServiceState[d]* – for each dependency‑service replica *d*, stores the set of commands that have already been learned and the dependencies that *d* believes each command has.  
* *PendingRequests* – the queue of client commands that have not yet been processed by the coordinator.  

**Safety Guarantees Expressed by the Invariants**

The model checks four invariants:

* **TypeOk** – ensures that every variable always holds a value of the expected type (e.g., sets of replicas, commands, integers). This prevents malformed states.
* **ConsensusConsistency** – guarantees that once an instance has been *chosen* (i.e., a command and its dependency set have been decided), every acceptor that later learns about that instance will agree on exactly the same command and dependency set. In other words, the protocol never decides two different values for the same instance.
* **Nontriviality** – asserts that a value can become chosen only if it was actually proposed by the coordinator (derived from a client’s command). The system cannot “invent” commands out of thin air.
* **ChosenConflicts** – enforces that if two commands conflict (as defined by the conflict relation between *a* and *b*), they cannot both be chosen for the same instance unless the chosen dependency sets impose a consistent ordering. This prevents the system from committing conflicting operations without respecting their mutual exclusion.

Together, these invariants capture the *safety* of the BPaxos protocol: decisions are unique, derived from genuine proposals, and respect the declared conflict relation.

---

**SAFETY PROPERTY:**  
The system guarantees that for every instance of the consensus protocol, at most one command can be chosen, and if a command is chosen its exact value (the command together with its dependency set) is the same for all replicas; furthermore, no two conflicting commands are ever both chosen without a dependency ordering that resolves the conflict. In plain terms, the protocol never decides contradictory or ambiguous commands, and any decision made is globally consistent and derived from an actual client request.

**System Overview**  
The specification models a small distributed computation composed of a fixed set of processes.  
The processes communicate by sending asynchronous messages to one another.  
The purpose of the model is to detect *global termination*: a state in which every process is idle, no messages are in transit, and every process has been accounted for by the termination‑detection algorithm.

**Variables**

| Variable | Meaning (in plain English) |
|----------|----------------------------|
| **s** | For every ordered pair *(i , j)* of processes, `s[i , j]` records how many messages process *i* has *sent* to process *j* so far. |
| **r** | For every ordered pair *(i , j)* of processes, `r[i , j]` records how many messages process *i* has *received* from process *j* so far. |
| **ds** | For every ordered pair *(i , j)*, `ds[i , j]` holds the *difference* between the number of messages that *i* believes it has sent to *j* and the number it believes *j* has acknowledged as received. In a correctly synchronised execution this value should always be non‑negative and becomes zero when the two sides agree. |
| **dr** | For every ordered pair *(i , j)*, `dr[i , j]` holds the analogous difference for the *receive* side: how many messages *i* thinks it has received from *j* minus the number *j* thinks it has sent to *i*. |
| **visited** | The set of processes that have already been incorporated into the termination‑detection spanning tree. A process enters this set when it first learns about the detection effort (for example, when it receives a “token” from its parent). |
| **terminated** | A Boolean flag that becomes true only when the algorithm has concluded that the whole system has terminated. Until that moment it stays false. |

**Actions (the possible state transitions)**  

1. **Init** – *system start*  
   * All counters `s`, `r`, `ds`, and `dr` are set to zero for every ordered pair of processes.  
   * The `visited` set is empty – no process has been added to the detection tree yet.  
   * `terminated` is false.  

2. **Send(i , j)** – *process *i* sends a message to process *j*  
   * The entry `s[i , j]` is incremented by one (recording that *i* has one more outbound message).  
   * The corresponding difference `ds[i , j]` is also incremented, reflecting that *i* now expects a matching receipt acknowledgment from *j*.  

3. **Receive(i , j)** – *process *i* receives a message that was sent by *j*  
   * The entry `r[i , j]` is incremented by one (recording that *i* has one more inbound message).  
   * The difference `dr[i , j]` is incremented, indicating that *i* now knows it has one more message that *j* claims to have sent.  

4. **Visit(i , parent)** – *process *i* becomes part of the detection tree*  
   * The process `i` is added to the `visited` set.  
   * Optionally, a parent‑child relationship is recorded implicitly (the parent is the process from which the “token” arrived). This relationship is used later for propagating termination information.  

5. **PropagateTermination(i)** – *process *i* informs its parent that it is locally quiescent*  
   * This action is enabled only when, for every neighbour *j*, both differences `ds[i , j]` and `dr[i , j]` are zero (i.e., all messages that *i* thinks it has sent have been acknowledged and all messages it thinks it has received have been accounted for).  
   * If *i* has children in the detection tree, it first waits until each child has already propagated its own termination.  
   * Once the local conditions are satisfied, *i* sends a “termination token” upward to its parent.  

6. **DetectTermination(root)** – *the root of the detection tree decides that the whole system has terminated*  
   * The root process may set `terminated` to true only when:  
     * Every process is in the `visited` set (the tree spans all processes).  
     * For every ordered pair *(i , j)*, both `ds[i , j]` and `dr[i , j]` are zero (no outstanding messages in either direction).  
   * After this action, the system remains in a stable state where no further `Send` or `Receive` actions are possible.  

**Safety Property**  
The invariant named **Canary1** guarantees that the system never reaches a state in which the `terminated` flag is true while there are still pending communications or unaccounted processes. In other words, the algorithm can only declare global termination when **all** processes have been incorporated into the detection tree **and** the send/receive counters for **every** pair of processes are perfectly balanced, meaning that no messages are in transit and no process is still active.  

**SAFETY PROPERTY:** The system may set the `terminated` flag to true only after every process has been visited and, for every ordered pair of processes, the number of messages sent equals the number of messages received; consequently, termination is never reported while any message is still in flight or any process remains unaccounted for.

**System Overview**

The model describes a small‑scale distributed agreement protocol that runs on a fixed collection of *consenters* (the participants) and proceeds in a bounded sequence of numbered *rounds*.  
Only two possible outcomes may be chosen – the values **x** or **y** – or the system may finish without ever selecting a value (the special value **none**).

**Key State Elements**

| Concept | Meaning in the implementation |
|---------|--------------------------------|
| **Rounds** | An integer counter that starts at 0 and is allowed to increase only up to a predetermined maximum (`MaxRound`). The set of admissible round numbers is therefore `{0, 1, 2, … , MaxRound}`. |
| **Consenters** | The finite set of nodes that can take part in the protocol (for the configuration shown: `{a, b, c}` ). |
| **Quorums** | A collection of subsets of consenters. Each subset is called a quorum; any quorum represents a group large enough to give the protocol authority. In the example, the quorums are `{a,b}`, `{b,c}` and `{a,c}`. |
| **Proposed value** | Each consenter may, in a given round, broadcast a proposal for either **x** or **y** (or the special sentinel **none** meaning “no proposal”). |
| **Votes / acknowledgements** | A consenter records the proposals it has received from other consenters and may acknowledge a proposal once it has heard from a quorum that supports the same value. |
| **Decided value** | Once a quorum of consenters have all acknowledged the same value in a round, that value becomes the *decided* value for the whole system. The decided value is stored in a global variable and never changes thereafter. |
| **Terminated flag** | A Boolean flag that becomes true when the protocol has either (i) reached a decided value or (ii) exhausted all allowed round numbers without reaching a decision. Once true, the system stops taking further actions. |

**Principal Actions (what the system can do in one step)**  

1. **Propose** – In any round that has not yet been terminated, any consenter may emit a proposal for **x** or **y** (or abstain, i.e., propose **none**). The proposal is recorded together with the round number.

2. **Collect** – A consenter examines the proposals it has received for the current round. If it sees that a *quorum* of consenters have all proposed the *same* value, it records that it has collected a quorum for that value.

3. **Decide** – When a consenter observes that a quorum for a particular value has been collected, it may trigger the *decision* action. This action writes the value into the global *decided* variable, marks the protocol as *decided*, and consequently sets the *terminated* flag.

4. **AdvanceRound** – If the current round finishes without a quorum being collected, any consenter may advance the round counter to the next integer, provided the new round number does not exceed `MaxRound`. When the counter reaches `MaxRound + 1` (i.e., there are no more admissible round numbers), the system automatically sets the *terminated* flag, signalling that the bounded run has ended without a decision.

5. **No‑op / Wait** – When the system is already terminated (either because a value has been decided or because the round bound has been hit), no further state changes occur; the model simply stays in the terminating state.

All actions are *fair* with respect to the global state: the model assumes that if an action remains enabled forever, it will eventually be taken. This is expressed by the fairness condition `WF_vars(Next)` in the TLA+ specification.

**Invariants (state‑consistency checks)**  

* **TypeOK** – Guarantees that every variable always holds a value of the expected type: round numbers stay within the finite range `0..MaxRound`, proposals and decided values are always one of `{x, y, none}`, sets of consenters and quorums are unchanged, and Boolean flags remain true/false.

* **Consistency** – Guarantees that the system never records two different decided values. At any reachable state, either no value has been decided yet, or exactly one value (either **x** or **y**) has been recorded as the decided value, and that value never changes thereafter.

**Temporal Goal**  

The model also checks that, along every execution, either the *Decided* action eventually becomes enabled (meaning a quorum has been reached and a value is recorded) or the *Terminated* action eventually becomes enabled (meaning the round bound has been exhausted). This captures the intended liveness property: the bounded run must finish either with a decision or with an explicit termination.

---

### SAFETY PROPERTY:
The system guarantees that it can never decide two different values; that is, if a value has been recorded as the decided outcome, no later step can record a different value, and the decided value remains immutable for the rest of the execution.

**System Overview**  
The specification models a very small instance of the classic Paxos consensus algorithm. It describes a group of three *acceptor* processes that cooperate to agree on a single *value* out of a predefined set of two possible values. The algorithm proceeds in logical “ballots” (also called proposal numbers) that are drawn from the set `{1, 2}`. A *quorum* is any subset of two acceptors; therefore every decision must be supported by at least two of the three acceptors.

---

### Constants (the fixed parts of the model)

| Name | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| **Values** | The set of admissible client values that may be chosen. In this model the two values are called `v1` and `v2`. |
| **Acceptors** | The three participants that run the Paxos acceptor role. They are identified as `a1`, `a2`, and `a3`. |
| **Quorums** | All subsets of acceptors that are large enough to decide a value. Because there are three acceptors, the model defines the three possible quorums `{a1,a2}`, `{a2,a3}`, and `{a3,a1}` – i.e., any two acceptors form a quorum. |
| **BallotNumbers** | The set of ballot identifiers that can be used when proposing a value. The model limits the search to the two numbers `1` and `2`. |
| **None** | A distinguished value meaning “no value has been chosen yet”. It is used to initialise variables that will later hold a concrete value. |

The symmetry definition tells the model checker that renaming values or acceptors does not change the behavior; this is only an optimisation for the checker and does not affect the logical description.

---

### Variables (the mutable state)

Although the TLA+ file does not list them explicitly, the imported *Paxos* module introduces the standard Paxos state variables:

| Variable | What it stores |
|----------|----------------|
| **promised[acceptor]** | For each acceptor, the highest ballot number it has promised not to reject. Initially `None`. |
| **accepted[acceptor]** | For each acceptor, a pair *(ballot, value)* that records the most recent value the acceptor has accepted together with the ballot number of that acceptance. Initially `(None, None)`. |
| **chosen** | The value that has been *decided* (i.e., learned) by the system, or `None` if no decision has been reached yet. |

These variables are updated only by the actions described below.

---

### Actions (the possible state transitions)

1. **Prepare(b, p)** – *proposer* sends a *prepare* message with ballot number `b` to a particular acceptor `p`.  
   *Effect*: If `b` is greater than the acceptor’s current `promised[p]`, the acceptor raises its promise to `b` and replies with the highest `(ballot, value)` pair it has accepted so far (or `None` if it has never accepted). Otherwise the acceptor ignores the request.

2. **Promise(p, b, lastAccepted)** – *acceptor* `p` records that it has promised not to accept any proposal with a ballot number smaller than `b`. The variable `promised[p]` becomes `b`. The reply `lastAccepted` is used by the proposer to decide which value to propose next.

3. **Propose(b, v)** – after gathering promises from a quorum, the *proposer* selects a value `v` to put forward in ballot `b`. The rule is the classic Paxos rule: if any acceptor in the quorum has already accepted a value, the proposer must adopt the value with the highest ballot among those; otherwise it may choose any value from `Values`.  

4. **Accept(p, b, v)** – the proposer sends an *accept* request to each acceptor `p` in the quorum with ballot `b` and value `v`.  
   *Effect*: If `b` is at least as large as `promised[p]`, the acceptor records the acceptance by setting `accepted[p] = (b, v)` and may later send a *learn* message. If `b` is smaller, the acceptor rejects the request.

5. **Learn(v)** – when a value `v` has been accepted by every member of some quorum, the system may mark the value as *chosen*. The variable `chosen` is set to `v`. Once `chosen` is non‑`None`, it never changes.

All actions are instantaneous logical steps; the model treats the network as reliable and messages as arriving in the order they are sent.

---

### Intended Behaviour

The protocol guarantees that:

* **Progress** – If a proposer repeatedly issues higher ballot numbers, eventually a quorum will accept a value and the system will move to a *chosen* state. (The model only checks safety, not liveness.)  
* **Consistency** – No two different values can ever be learned (chosen) by the system, even if several proposers operate concurrently and ballots are interleaved.

The invariant in the specification captures the second point.

---

### SAFETY PROPERTY:  
The system never reaches a state in which two distinct values have been chosen; that is, once a value has been recorded as the decided (chosen) value, every later state either has the same chosen value or still has no chosen value. Consequently, the algorithm guarantees uniqueness of the consensus decision.

**System Overview**

The model describes a tiny thread‑pool system that executes a fixed set of work items using a fixed set of worker threads. It is deliberately small – exactly three distinct threads and three distinct items – so that every possible interaction can be explored exhaustively by the model checker.

---

### Core Entities  

| Entity | Meaning in the system |
|--------|-----------------------|
| **Threads** (`t1`, `t2`, `t3`) | Three independent worker threads. Each thread can be idle or busy processing a single item at a time. |
| **Items** (`i1`, `i2`, `i3`) | Three distinct units of work that must be processed exactly once. An item can be **waiting**, **in progress**, or **finished**. |
| **ItemPool** | The collection of items that have not yet been taken by any thread (the “waiting queue”). |
| **BusyMap** | A mapping that records, for each thread that is currently busy, which item it is processing. |
| **DoneSet** | The set of items that have already completed processing. |

All of these structures are kept in memory as ordinary variables; the model checker guarantees that they always contain only the defined thread and item identifiers.

---

### Behaviour (Actions)

The system evolves by repeatedly executing one of the following atomic actions. Each action represents a single step that a real implementation could perform.

1. **StartProcessing** – *A free thread picks up a waiting item*  
   *Pre‑condition*: There exists at least one idle thread and at least one item in the waiting pool.  
   *Effect*: The selected thread is marked as busy, the chosen item is removed from the waiting pool, and the thread‑to‑item mapping is updated to reflect that the thread is now processing that item.

2. **FinishProcessing** – *A busy thread finishes its current work*  
   *Pre‑condition*: A thread is currently busy with some item.  
   *Effect*: The item is moved from the busy mapping to the finished set, and the thread becomes idle again. The mapping entry for that thread is cleared.

3. **NoOp** – *The system may also stay idle*  
   *Pre‑condition*: None (the model permits stuttering steps).  
   *Effect*: No state variables change; this action exists only to satisfy the fairness requirements of the model checker.

These three actions together capture the life‑cycle of each item: it starts in the waiting pool, is taken by exactly one thread, and after the thread finishes it moves to the completed set. No other state changes are possible.

---

### Type Invariant (`TypeOk`)

The first invariant asserts that every variable always contains values of the expected kind:

* The waiting pool always contains only the three declared items, never any other identifier.  
* The busy mapping always associates each busy thread with exactly one of the declared items, and never with a non‑existent item.  
* The done set always contains only declared items, and never any thread identifiers.  
* The three thread constants remain distinct, and likewise the three item constants remain distinct.

In short, the model never “goes off the rails” by storing an unexpected value.

---

### Duplicate‑Processing Invariant (`NoItemIsProcessedInDuplicate`)

The second invariant captures the core safety requirement of a thread pool: **no work item may be processed by more than one thread at the same time**. Formally, at any reachable state the set of items currently assigned to busy threads is a set (i.e., contains no duplicates). Equivalently, if two different threads are busy, the items they are working on must be different.

This invariant is checked after every possible transition, guaranteeing that the system never reaches a state where two threads are simultaneously working on the same item.

---

## SAFETY PROPERTY:
The system guarantees that at no point during its execution can the same work item be processed by more than one thread simultaneously; each item, while it is being worked on, is assigned to at most one thread.

CONSTANTS
    THREADS = {t1, t2, t3}
    ITEMS   = {i1, i2, i3}
    NONE    = None

INIT Init
NEXT Next
INVARIANT NoItemDuplicateProcessing

**System Overview**

The model describes a very small asynchronous communication link that connects a single sender to a single receiver. The link is represented by one shared data structure called **the channel**.

* **Channel contents** – The channel holds three pieces of information:
  1. **Value** – the actual data item that the sender wants to deliver. The value must always be one of the elements of a predefined set called **Data** (for example `{1,2}` in the supplied configuration).
  2. **Ready flag** – a binary flag (0 or 1) that is used by the sender to indicate that a new value has been placed in the channel.
  3. **Acknowledge flag** – another binary flag (0 or 1) that is used by the receiver to confirm that it has taken the value out of the channel.

* **Initial state** – At system start the channel is empty of meaningful data (its `value` can be any element of `Data`) and the two flags are equal (`ready = ack`). Equality of the flags means that no new data is awaiting acknowledgment; the link is idle.

* **Sender action – “Send(d)”**  
  - **Prerequisite** – The sender may act only when the channel is idle, i.e., when `ready` and `ack` are equal.  
  - **Effect** – The sender writes the chosen data item `d` into the channel’s `value` field and then flips the `ready` flag (changing 0 to 1 or 1 to 0). The `ack` flag is left unchanged. Flipping `ready` makes it different from `ack`, signalling to the receiver that fresh data is now available.

* **Receiver action – “Receive”**  
  - **Prerequisite** – The receiver may act only when the channel holds unacknowledged data, i.e., when `ready` and `ack` differ.  
  - **Effect** – The receiver toggles the `ack` flag (changing 0 to 1 or 1 to 0) while leaving the other fields unchanged. After this toggle, `ready` and `ack` become equal again, indicating that the receiver has successfully taken the data and the channel returns to the idle state.

* **System dynamics** – In each step the system may either perform a `Send` of any data element from `Data` (if the channel is idle) or perform a `Receive` (if data is pending). The specification requires that the system repeatedly executes such steps forever, modeling an ongoing handshake between sender and receiver.

**Safety Property**

SAFETY PROPERTY: The channel always contains a data value that belongs to the predefined Data set, and both the ready flag and the acknowledgment flag are always binary (either 0 or 1). This invariant guarantees that the channel never holds an illegal data value and that the control flags remain well‑formed throughout the execution.

INIT Init
NEXT Next
INVARIANT ChannelInvariant

nl:
**System Overview**

The model describes a tiny distributed consensus service that implements the core of the Paxos algorithm.  
It contains exactly two *participants* (named p1 and p2) that act as both proposers and acceptors, and a single *consensus instance* in which the participants must agree on one of two possible *values* (named v1 and v2).

The system is represented by a small set of state variables that capture the information each participant holds about the ongoing Paxos round and the value that may eventually be committed.

| Variable | Meaning |
|----------|---------|
| **round[p]** (for each participant *p*) | The current proposal number (a natural number) that the participant has promised not to accept any proposal with a smaller number. |
| **vote[p]** (for each participant *p*) | The value that the participant has most recently accepted, together with the round number of that acceptance. If the participant has not yet accepted anything, the entry is *None*. |
| **store** | The globally visible log entry that records the *decided* value for the consensus instance. It is *None* while no value has been decided, and becomes either *v1* or *v2* once a majority (here, both participants) have accepted the same value in the same round. |
| **maxRound** | The highest round number that any participant has seen so far; it is used to generate new, larger proposal numbers. |

All variables are initialized to the lowest round (0), with no votes and an empty store.

---

**Actions (State Transitions)**  

1. **Prepare(p)** – *p* starts a new Paxos round.  
   *p* picks a round number larger than **maxRound**, updates its own **round[p]** to that number, and broadcasts a *prepare* request containing the new round number to the other participant.

2. **Promise(q, r, v)** – When participant *q* receives a *prepare* request with round *r*, it checks whether *r* is greater than its current **round[q]**.  
   * If the check succeeds, **round[q]** is set to *r* and *q* replies with a *promise* that includes the last value it has voted for (the pair **vote[q]**, which may be *None*).  
   * If the check fails, *q* ignores the request (no state change).

3. **Accept(p, r, v)** – After receiving promises from a majority (both participants in this model), *p* selects a value to propose:  
   * If any promise carried a previously accepted value, *p* must propose the highest‑numbered such value; otherwise it may propose any client‑requested value *v* (v1 or v2).  
   * *p* then sends an *accept* message containing the round *r* and the chosen value *v* to the other participant.

4. **Learn(q, r, v)** – When participant *q* receives an *accept* request with round *r* and value *v*, it checks that *r* is at least as large as **round[q]**.  
   * If the check succeeds, **vote[q]** is set to the pair (r, v) and **round[q]** is updated to *r*.  
   * If both participants now have **vote[·]** equal to the same pair (r, v), the **store** is updated to *v*, meaning the value is *decided*.

5. **ClientRequest(p, v)** – A client can ask any participant *p* to start a consensus on value *v*. The request simply triggers the *Prepare* action for *p*; the actual value *v* is used only if no prior accepted value is carried in the promises.

All actions are atomic with respect to the model – each transition represents the receipt of a message and the corresponding local update.

---

**Safety Property (Invariant)**  

The invariant guarantees the fundamental safety condition of Paxos: *once a value has been decided, no other different value can ever be decided for the same consensus instance.* In other words, the system never reaches a state where the global store contains two distinct values, nor can it later change a decided value to a different one. This ensures that all participants agree on a single, immutable result for the instance, regardless of the ordering or timing of messages.  

**SAFETY PROPERTY:**  
At any reachable state, it is never the case that two different values have been recorded as decided for the consensus instance; if the store holds a value (v1 or v2), that value is the only one that can ever be stored, and no other value can become stored thereafter.

**System Overview**

The model describes a classic coordination problem involving a small group of prisoners who are allowed to enter a single, isolated room one at a time. Inside the room there is a single binary device – for example a light bulb that can be either **off** or **on**. The prisoners must eventually reach a state in which one of them (the *leader*) can be certain that every prisoner has entered the room at least once, without any external communication other than the state of the light.

The model is parameterised with two constants:

* **Number of prisoners** – the set `{1, 2, 3, 4}`. Thus there are exactly four distinct prisoners, each identified by a unique number.
* **Counter** – a natural‑number constant whose initial value is `1`. This constant is used by the leader as the target value that the internal counter must reach before the leader may declare that all prisoners have visited.

The dynamic state of the system consists of three logical variables (these are defined inside the imported `APAPrisoners` module):

1. **CurrentPrisoner** – the identifier of the prisoner that is presently inside the room. At each step a different prisoner may be chosen nondeterministically.
2. **Light** – a Boolean flag representing the state of the bulb (`on` or `off`). The bulb is the only shared memory that the prisoners can observe and modify.
3. **SeenCount** – a non‑negative integer that the leader updates whenever she observes the bulb turned on. It starts at `0` and is increased by one each time the leader turns the bulb off.

**Behavioural Actions**

The system evolves by repeatedly executing one of the following actions, each triggered when a particular prisoner enters the room:

* **LeaderVisit** – the designated leader (prisoner 1, for instance) enters the room.
  * If the bulb is **on**, the leader turns it **off** and increments `SeenCount` by one.
  * If the bulb is **off**, the leader leaves it unchanged and does not modify `SeenCount`.

* **NonLeaderVisit** – any non‑leader prisoner (prisoners 2, 3, 4) enters the room.
  * Each non‑leader maintains a private flag “hasSignalled” that is initially **false**.
  * When a non‑leader finds the bulb **off** and his private flag is **false**, he turns the bulb **on** and sets his flag to **true** (signalling that he has visited at least once).
  * In all other situations (bulb already on, or his flag already true) he leaves the bulb unchanged.

The selection of the next prisoner is completely nondeterministic, modelling the fact that the prison guard decides who may enter next without any pattern.

**Safety Goal (Invariant)**  

The invariant labelled `SafetyInv` captures the essential safety requirement of the protocol:

*The leader can never reach the target counter value (the constant **Counter**) unless every prisoner has already visited the room at least once.*

In other words, the system guarantees that the condition “`SeenCount` equals the constant Counter” is **only** true in states where each of the four prisoners’s private “hasSignalled’’ flag is true. Consequently, the leader will never incorrectly announce that all prisoners have visited.

---

**SAFETY PROPERTY:**  
It is never possible for the leader’s internal counter to reach the predefined target value unless every prisoner has entered the room at least once; thus the leader can only declare that all prisoners have visited when that fact is indeed true.

CONSTANTS
    Prisoners = {1, 2, 3, 4}
    Leader = 1
    Counter = 3

NEXT Next
INVARIANT SafetyInv

nl:
**System Overview**

The specification models a small‑scale Paxos‑style consensus protocol that is used to agree on a single value among a group of *acceptors*.  

* **Acceptors** – The system contains four permanent participants identified as **a1, a2, a3, and a4**.  Each acceptor stores two pieces of information:
  * the *highest ballot number* it has promised not to reject (the *promise*), and  
  * the *value* it has most recently accepted together with the ballot at which it was accepted.  

* **Values** – Two possible application values can be chosen, called **v1** and **v2**.  No other values exist in the model.

* **Ballots** – The protocol proceeds in numbered rounds called *ballots*.  Ballot numbers are drawn from the finite set {0, 1, 2}.  Higher numbers dominate lower numbers.

* **Quorums** – To make progress a proposer must obtain responses from a *quorum* of acceptors.  Two families of quorums are defined:
  * **Phase‑1 quorums** (named *Quorum1*) consist of either the pair {a1, a2} or the pair {a3, a4}.  A proposer can collect a Phase‑1 quorum by contacting either of these two disjoint pairs.
  * **Phase‑2 quorums** (named *Quorum2*) consist of either the pair {a1, a3} or the pair {a2, a4}.  A proposer can collect a Phase‑2 quorum by contacting either of these two alternative pairs.

  The two families are deliberately chosen so that *any* Phase‑1 quorum intersects *any* Phase‑2 quorum in at least one acceptor.  This intersection guarantees the classic Paxos safety property.

* **Proposers** – The model includes an arbitrary number of proposers (the exact identifier set is not fixed).  Each proposer maintains:
  * a *current ballot* it is trying to run,
  * a *candidate value* it wishes to have chosen, and
  * a flag that indicates whether it has already learned a chosen value.

* **Chosen value set** – A global set records the values that have been *decided* (i.e., learned by a majority of acceptors).  The set may contain at most one element because the protocol is intended to decide a single value.

**Protocol Actions**

1. **StartPrepare (Phase 1 – Prepare)**  
   A proposer selects a new ballot number that is greater than any ballot it has used before and sends a *prepare* request to all acceptors in a Phase‑1 quorum.  

2. **ReceivePromise (Phase 1 – Promise)**  
   An acceptor that receives a prepare request with a ballot higher than any ballot it has already promised updates its promise to that ballot and replies with:
   * the ballot it has already promised (now equal to the new one), and  
   * the *most recent* (ballot, value) pair it has accepted, if any.  

3. **SelectValue (Phase 1 – Value Decision)**  
   Once a proposer has collected promises from a complete Phase‑1 quorum, it examines the accepted pairs reported by the quorum:
   * If at least one acceptor reported an accepted value, the proposer adopts the value belonging to the *highest* reported ballot.  
   * If none reported an accepted value, the proposer may choose any value from the application set {v1, v2}.  

4. **StartAccept (Phase 2 – Accept)**  
   The proposer now sends an *accept* request containing its current ballot and the value selected in the previous step to all acceptors in a Phase‑2 quorum.

5. **ReceiveAccept (Phase 2 – Acceptance)**  
   An acceptor that receives an accept request with a ballot that matches its current promise records the (ballot, value) pair as its latest accepted entry and replies with an acknowledgement.

6. **Learn (Decision)**  
   When a proposer gathers acknowledgements from a full Phase‑2 quorum, it concludes that the value has been *chosen*.  It adds that value to the global chosen‑value set and may broadcast the decision to all participants.

7. **No‑op / Retry**  
   If a proposer discovers that a received promise or accept acknowledgement contains a higher ballot than the one it is using, it aborts the current attempt, increments its ballot, and restarts the prepare phase.  This captures the “higher‑ballot” pre‑emptive behavior required by Paxos.

**State‑type Constraints (TypeOK)**  

The model also checks that every variable always holds a value of the correct type:
* Ballot numbers are always within the range 0‑2.  
* Values stored in acceptors or proposals are always either **v1** or **v2** (or a special “None” placeholder before any value is chosen).  
* Quorum collections contain only the defined acceptor identifiers.  

**Safety Guarantee (Invariant)**  

The invariant named **SafeValue** expresses the core safety property of Paxos: once a value has been recorded as chosen, no other distinct value can ever be recorded as chosen in any later state.  Because every Phase‑1 quorum overlaps every Phase‑2 quorum, any two decisions must share at least one acceptor, and that acceptor can only accept one value for the highest ballot it has promised.  Consequently, all decisions are forced to be the same value.

---

**SAFETY PROPERTY:**  
At any point in the execution, if a value has been decided (added to the global chosen‑value set), then that value is the only value that can ever be decided; no two different values can both be chosen, and any decided value must be one of the application values **v1** or **v2**.

**System Overview** The model describes a classic *two‑phase commit* protocol that coordinates a set of independent resource managers (RMs). The constant set **RM** contains the identifiers of the participating RMs – in this instance the seven managers `r1` through `r7`. The protocol is driven by a single coordinator that interacts with the RMs to reach a unanimous decision to either **commit** the transaction or **abort** it. --- ### Main State Variables | Variable (concept) | Meaning in the implementation | |--------------------|--------------------------------| | **rmState** (a map from each RM to a status) | For every resource manager the variable records which phase it is in. The possible statuses are:
• **Working** – the RM is executing the transaction but has not yet been asked to prepare.
• **Prepared** – the RM has finished its work, is ready to commit, and has replied positively to the coordinator.
• **Committed** – the RM has applied the transaction permanently.
• **Aborted** – the RM has rolled back the transaction. | | **coordState** | The current phase of the coordinator. It can be:
• **Init** – before any work has started.
• **Waiting** – the coordinator has sent *prepare* messages and is collecting votes.
• **CommitDecision** – the coordinator has decided to commit (all votes were positive).
• **AbortDecision** – the coordinator has decided to abort (at least one negative vote). | | **votes** (optional auxiliary map) | Records, for each RM, whether a *yes* (prepare‑ok) or *no* (prepare‑abort) vote has been received. This auxiliary variable is only used internally by the protocol logic. | All variables are initialized by the **Init** action and are subsequently changed only by the actions defined in **Next**. --- ### Actions (protocol steps) 1. **Init** – *system start* * All RMs are set to the **Working** state. * The coordinator is placed in the **Init** state. * No votes have been recorded yet. 2. **PrepareRequest** – *coordinator asks each RM to prepare* * The coordinator moves from **Init** to **Waiting**. * It sends a *prepare* message to every RM (conceptually; the model simply makes the RMs eligible to respond). 3. **RMPrepare** – *an individual RM responds positively* * An RM that is currently **Working** can receive the prepare request and change its status to **Prepared**. * The RM records a **yes** vote in the auxiliary `votes` map. 4. **RMAbort** – *an individual RM cannot prepare and votes to abort* * An RM that is **Working** may instead decide it cannot commit (e.g., due to a local error) and immediately move to **Aborted**. * It records a **no** vote. 5. **CoordinatorDecision** – *the coordinator decides after collecting votes* * If **all** RMs have recorded a **yes** vote (i.e., every RM is in **Prepared**), the coordinator changes to **CommitDecision**. * If **any** RM has recorded a **no** vote (i.e., at least one RM is **Aborted**), the coordinator changes to **AbortDecision**. 6. **CommitBroadcast** – *the coordinator tells RMs to commit* * When the coordinator is in **CommitDecision**, it sends a commit command to every RM. * Each RM that is in **Prepared** changes its state to **Committed**. 7. **AbortBroadcast** – *the coordinator tells RMs to abort* * When the coordinator is in **AbortDecision**, it sends an abort command to every RM. * Any RM that is still **Prepared** or **Working** moves to **Aborted**. 8. **Recovery / No‑op steps** – *the model also allows steps where no state changes occur, representing waiting or message delays.* All of the above steps are captured by the single `Next` action in the specification; each step is nondeterministically chosen at each state transition, modelling the asynchronous nature of distributed communication. --- ### Safety Goal (Invariant) The invariant named **TCConsistent** expresses the fundamental safety requirement of the two‑phase commit protocol: the system must never reach a state where some resource managers have permanently committed the transaction while others have rolled it back. In other words, the final decision must be globally consistent. **SAFETY PROPERTY:** *At any reachable moment, it is impossible for one resource manager to be in the **Committed** state while another is in the **Aborted** state. Moreover, if the coordinator has decided to commit, then every resource manager must eventually be in the **Committed** state; if the coordinator has decided to abort, then no resource manager may ever be in the **Committed** state.*

**System Overview**  
The model describes a small real‑time component that maintains a collection of four integer “clocks”.  Each clock records a non‑negative count that can be increased, reset, or left unchanged as the system evolves.  The clocks are identified by the names **c0**, **c1**, **c2**, and **c3**.  A global bound limits how large any clock is allowed to become; if a clock tries to exceed that bound an error is recorded.  The system also keeps a counter of how many such errors have occurred, and the counter is itself limited by a maximum error value.

---

### Variables  

| Variable | Meaning |
|----------|---------|
| **clocks** | A mapping that stores the current integer value of each of the four clocks (c0 … c3). All values are always ≥ 0. |
| **errCnt** | An integer that counts how many times a clock has been observed to exceed the permitted bound. It is never negative. |
| **maxErr** | A constant (taken from the configuration) that is the absolute ceiling for **errCnt**. The model never permits the counter to go above this value. |
| **bound** | A constant (taken from the configuration) that is the maximum admissible value for any individual clock. |

---

### Initialization  

When the system starts, every clock is set to **0** and the error counter is also **0**.  This represents a clean start with no elapsed time and no violations recorded.

---

### State‑transition (Next)  

At each logical step the system may perform one of several nondeterministic actions:

1. **Increment a Clock** – The system chooses one of the four clocks and adds **1** to its current value.  
2. **Reset a Clock** – The system chooses one of the four clocks and sets its value back to **0** (for example, to model a timer being cleared).  
3. **No‑op** – The system may also decide to leave all clocks unchanged for a step.  

After the chosen update, the model checks the *bound* condition:

*If the updated value of any clock is greater than the configured **bound**, the system records an error*:  
* the offending clock is immediately reset to **0** (so the system never stays in a state where a clock exceeds the bound), and  
* the global error counter **errCnt** is increased by **1**, but never beyond the configured **maxErr** (the counter is saturated at that limit).

Thus the transition logic both advances the clocks and enforces the safety envelope defined by the bound.

---

### Invariant (Safety condition being checked)  

The invariant that the model checker verifies can be read as two complementary guarantees that must hold in **every reachable state**:

1. **Clock‑range guarantee** – Each of the four clocks always holds a value that lies in the closed interval **[0, bound]**.  The system never allows a clock to remain outside this range.  
2. **Error‑counter guarantee** – The accumulated error count **errCnt** never exceeds the configured maximum **maxErr**.  Even if many bound violations occur, the counter is capped and the model guarantees that the cap is never overrun.

Together, these conditions assure that the system’s timing variables stay within their prescribed limits and that the bookkeeping of bound violations remains bounded.

---

**SAFETY PROPERTY:**  
In every possible execution, each clock’s integer value is always between zero and the configured bound, and the total number of recorded bound‑exceeding errors never grows larger than the configured maximum error count.
cfg_text:
CONSTANT bound = 5
CONSTANT maxErr = 3

INVARIANT Safety

nl:
**System Overview**

The model describes a tiny distributed‑time subsystem that consists of eight independent logical clocks, named *c0* through *c7*.  
Each clock holds a non‑negative integer value that represents its current “tick count”.  
In addition to the clocks, the system maintains a single global error counter.

All integer values are limited by two constants supplied to the model:

* **BOUND** – the maximum allowed value for any clock (here the bound is 10).  
* **ERRMAX** – the maximum allowed value for the global error counter (also 10).

---

**State Variables**

| Variable | Meaning |
|----------|---------|
| **ClockValues** | A table that maps each clock identifier (*c0* … *c7*) to its current integer value. |
| **ErrCount** | A single integer that records how many error events have occurred so far. |

Initially every entry in **ClockValues** is set to 0 and **ErrCount** is also 0.

---

**Actions (State Transitions)**  

The system evolves by repeatedly applying one of the following kinds of steps:

1. **Clock Tick** – Choose any one of the eight clocks. If its current value is strictly less than **BOUND**, increase that clock’s value by exactly one. All other clocks and the error counter remain unchanged.

2. **Error Event** – If the global error counter is strictly less than **ERRMAX**, increase **ErrCount** by one. Clock values are left untouched.

3. **No‑op / Stuttering** – The model also permits a step that leaves all variables unchanged, which represents the passage of time without any observable event.

These actions together constitute the *Next* relation: at each step the system nondeterministically picks one of the permissible actions and updates the state accordingly, obeying the numeric limits described above.

---

**Safety Property (Invariant)**  

The invariant that the model checker must preserve is two‑fold:

* Every clock’s value is always within the closed interval from 0 up to **BOUND** (inclusive).  
* The global error counter is always within the closed interval from 0 up to **ERRMAX** (inclusive).

In other words, the system never allows a clock to “overflow” beyond the configured bound, and it never lets the error counter exceed its maximum allowed value.

---

**SAFETY PROPERTY:**  
At all reachable states, each of the eight clocks holds an integer between 0 and 10, and the error counter holds an integer between 0 and 10; the system never violates these limits.

**System Overview**  
The model describes a tiny real‑time component that contains two independent logical clocks, named **c0** and **c1**.  
Each clock records an integer “tick count” that grows as time passes.  
The component also keeps a single *error counter* that records how many times the two clocks have become too far apart.  
All numeric values are bounded by constants supplied to the model: the clocks may never exceed **BOUND = 9**, and the error counter may never exceed **ERRMAX = 10**.

---

**State Variables**

| Variable | Meaning |
|----------|---------|
| **clock** (a mapping from clock identifiers to integers) | For each identifier `c0` and `c1`, the current integer value of that logical clock. The value represents how many ticks have occurred since that clock was last reset. |
| **err** (integer) | A non‑negative counter that is incremented each time the difference between the two clocks exceeds the allowed bound. It is never allowed to grow beyond `ERRMAX`. |

---

**Initial State (Init)**  
When the system starts, both clocks are set to zero and the error counter is also zero. In other words, the component begins in a perfectly synchronized state with no recorded errors.

---

**Possible State Transitions (Next)**  

1. **Tick a Clock**  
   *Choose one of the two clocks (c0 or c1) and increase its value by one.*  
   This models the passage of one unit of logical time for that clock. The increment is allowed only while the resulting value stays within the global bound (≤ 9). If the clock is already at the bound, the tick action is not enabled for that clock.

2. **Reset a Clock**  
   *Choose one of the two clocks and set its value back to zero.*  
   This models an explicit re‑initialisation of that clock (for example, after it has been used to measure a duration). The reset can be performed at any moment, regardless of the clock’s current value.

3. **Detect a Bound Violation**  
   *Examine the two clocks; if the absolute difference between their values is larger than the configured bound (9), increment the error counter by one.*  
   The error counter is increased only when a violation is observed. The increment is permitted only while the counter remains ≤ ERRMAX; when the counter would exceed ERRMAX the transition is disabled, effectively preventing the system from entering a state with too many violations.

All three actions are nondeterministic – at each step the environment may decide which enabled action (if any) occurs.

---

**Safety Property (Invariant)**  

The invariant that the model checks expresses two things that must always hold, no matter how the system evolves:

* every clock value stays inside the allowed range **0 … BOUND** (i.e., never becomes negative or larger than 9), and  
* the error counter never exceeds the configured maximum **ERRMAX** (i.e., it is always 0 … 10).

These conditions together guarantee that the component never drifts outside its numeric limits and that the number of observed clock‑difference violations is bounded.

**SAFETY PROPERTY:**  
At all times, each clock’s integer value is between 0 and BOUND (inclusive), and the error counter never exceeds ERRMAX.
cfg_text:
CONSTANTS
    BOUND = 9
    ERRMAX = 10
    Clocks = {"c0", "c1"}

nl:
**System Overview**

The model describes a small embedded‑timing subsystem that maintains six independent integer “clocks”.  
Each clock records how many logical time units have elapsed since that clock was last reset.  
The clocks are named **c0, c1, c2, c3, c4, and c5**.  

All clocks are **bounded**: a clock value is never allowed to grow beyond the constant **BOUND = 9**.  
When a clock would be incremented past this bound, the system does not allow the illegal value; instead it records an **error**.  
A global error counter, called **err**, counts how many times a bound‑violation has been attempted.  
The counter itself is limited by the constant **ERRMAX = 10** – the system is considered to have failed if more than ten such violations occur.

The model is completely deterministic apart from the choice of which clock to act on at each step; the choice is nondeterministic in the sense that the model checker explores all possibilities.

---

### Variables

| Variable | Meaning |
|----------|---------|
| **c0 … c5** | Integer value of each logical clock. Each value is always ≥ 0. |
| **err** | Global error counter that records the number of times a clock increment was blocked because it would have exceeded the bound. |
| **clkSet** (implicit) | The fixed set `{c0, c1, c2, c3, c4, c5}`; it never changes. |

---

### Initialization (Init)

When the system starts:

1. Every clock **c0 … c5** is set to **0**.  
2. The error counter **err** is set to **0**.  

Thus the system begins in a perfectly synchronized state with no elapsed time and no recorded errors.

---

### Transition Relation (Next)

At each logical step the system performs exactly one of the following actions, chosen nondeterministically:

1. **Tick a Clock**  
   *Select a clock `ci` from the set `{c0,…,c5}`.*  
   - If the current value of `ci` is **strictly less than BOUND (9)**, the clock is incremented by **1** (i.e., `ci := ci + 1`).  
   - If the current value of `ci` is **already equal to BOUND**, the increment is **blocked**; the clock stays at 9 and the global error counter is increased by **1** (`err := err + 1`).  

2. **Reset a Clock**  
   *Select a clock `ci` from the set `{c0,…,c5}`.*  
   - The chosen clock is set back to **0** (`ci := 0`).  
   - The error counter is **unchanged**.  

No other variables are modified during a step. The action “tick” represents the passage of one logical time unit for the selected clock, while “reset” models an external event that restarts the clock (for example, the completion of a task).

---

### Invariant (Inv)

The invariant is a condition that must hold after **every** reachable state of the system. It consists of two parts:

1. **Clock‑Bound Safety** – Every clock value is always within the closed interval **[0, BOUND]**, i.e., no clock ever holds a negative number or a number larger than 9.  

2. **Error‑Counter Limit** – The global error counter **err** never exceeds **ERRMAX**; it is always **≤ 10**.  

These two constraints together guarantee that the system never enters an illegal state where a clock value is out of range, and that the number of bound‑violation attempts remains bounded.

---

### Behavior Summary

- The system starts with all clocks at zero and no errors.  
- At each step a single clock is either advanced by one tick (if doing so respects the bound) or reset to zero.  
- If a tick would violate the bound, the tick is suppressed and the error counter is incremented.  
- The model checker explores all possible sequences of ticks and resets across the six clocks.  
- The invariant ensures that, regardless of the nondeterministic choices, the clocks never exceed the bound and the error counter never grows beyond ten.

---

**SAFETY PROPERTY:**  
The system always maintains every clock value between 0 and 9 inclusive, and the global error counter never exceeds 10. In other words, no clock ever overflows its prescribed bound, and the number of attempted overflows is limited to ten.

**System Overview**

The model describes a simple data‑store that can hold a collection of distinct items drawn from a fixed catalogue of fifteen possible values.  

* **Catalogue of values** – The constant `values` is the set `{v0, v1, …, v14}`. These are the only identifiers that are ever allowed to appear in the store.  

* **State variable** – The system’s state is captured by a single variable (often called `S` or `store`). It is a set that contains the items that have already been inserted. Because it is a set, each element can be present at most once.

* **Initial state** – When the system starts, the store is empty; no catalogue element has been added yet.

* **Transition (Add action)** – The only possible step the system can take is to add a new element:
  1. Choose any catalogue value that is **not already** in the store.
  2. Insert that value into the store, leaving all previously stored values unchanged.
  3. The step is nondeterministic – any admissible value may be chosen, but only one value is added per step.
  4. No removal or other mutation of the store is possible.

* **Behaviour** – Because the store only grows, the system can perform at most fifteen add steps before it reaches a state where every catalogue value is present. After that point no further transition is enabled (the model simply deadlocks, which is acceptable for the safety analysis).

**Safety Property**

The invariant that the model checks guarantees two things at every reachable state:

* The contents of the store are always a subset of the predefined catalogue; no value outside `{v0,…,v14}` can ever appear.
* Each catalogue value appears at most once, i.e., the store never contains duplicate entries, and consequently its cardinality never exceeds fifteen.

These conditions together ensure that the system never stores an illegal or duplicated item.

**SAFETY PROPERTY:**  
At all times the store is a subset of the fixed set `{v0,…,v14}` and contains no duplicate elements; therefore its size never exceeds 15.

**System Overview**

The model describes a simple mutable collection that can hold any of a fixed list of identifiers, namely the strings “v0” through “v17”.  
The collection is represented by a single variable that we will call **the current set**.  
The set may be empty, may contain one element, or may contain many elements, but it can never hold something that is not one of the identifiers listed above.

**Initial State**

When the system starts, the current set is empty. No identifiers are present in the collection at the beginning of execution.

**State‑Transition Actions (the “Next” step)**  

At each discrete step the system nondeterministically chooses one of two possible actions:

1. **Add** – The system picks one identifier from the predefined list that is **not already** in the current set and inserts it.  
   *Effect*: the chosen identifier becomes a member of the set; all other members remain unchanged.

2. **Delete** – The system picks one identifier that **is already** in the current set and removes it.  
   *Effect*: the chosen identifier is no longer a member of the set; all other members remain unchanged.

If the set is already full (contains every identifier) the *Add* action is unavailable; if the set is empty the *Delete* action is unavailable. Apart from these constraints, the choice of which identifier to add or delete is completely nondeterministic.

**Safety Property (Invariant)**  

The invariant that the model checker verifies states that, at every reachable state of the system, the current set consists only of identifiers drawn from the predefined list and never contains any element outside that list. In other words, the set is always a subset of the allowed values, guaranteeing that no illegal or unknown value can ever be introduced.

**SAFETY PROPERTY:**  
The collection never contains a value that is not one of the predefined identifiers “v0” … “v17”; the set is always a subset of the allowed values.
